extracted.intended_audience: registered patent attorneys/agents and practitioners subject to USPTO reciprocal disciplinary proceedings; OED staff and counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria used by the USPTO Director to decide whether to impose identical reciprocal discipline under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 based on a state's disciplinary determination, and the defenses a respondent must show to avoid identical discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imposition of identical discipline under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates and the Director finds there is a genuine issue of material fact as to one of the listed exceptions in § 11.24(d)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office will generally apply the same form of public discipline imposed by the state (i.e., identical sanction) unless a narrow, statutory exception is established by the respondent. The cited exceptions are set out in § 11.24(d)(1) and mirror the Selling v. Radford standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of reciprocity (Selling v. Radford) and respondent's burden
rubrics_metrics.description: A state suspension creates a federal-level presumption that imposition of reciprocal discipline is proper; the respondent must demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that one of the Selling elements precludes reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal/USPTO review is narrow — the Director is not sitting as a court of review to discover error. Case law (e.g., In re Kramer, In re Friedman, In re Zdravkovich) supports that the respondent bears the burden to show a genuine issue of material fact by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground (i): Deprivation of due process
rubrics_metrics.description: The procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due process requires reasonable notice of charges and a meaningful opportunity to be heard (e.g., present evidence, testify, cross-examine witnesses). Mere disagreement with evidentiary rulings or a lost evidentiary dispute (e.g., denial of a subpoena) ordinarily does not establish deprivation of due process absent a showing that rulings prevented a fair opportunity to present a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground (ii): Infirmity of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: There was such an infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(ii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a difficult showing: deference is generally given to the trier-of-fact's credibility determinations. A respondent's mere disagreement with findings or credibility assessments is insufficient. The Office looks for clear evidentiary infirmities that would render the state's conclusion unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground (iii): Grave injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: Disbarment, suspension or disciplinary disqualification by the Office would result in a grave injustice (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis focuses on whether the severity of the punishment 'fits' the misconduct. The standard is high: the respondent must show reciprocal discipline would be so ill-fitted as to be a grave injustice. The Office compares sanctions to ranges in authoritative guidance (e.g., ABA Standards) and reviews mitigating/aggravating circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground (iv): Practitioner was not publicly disciplined
rubrics_metrics.description: Any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iv)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the state action was not one of the listed public disciplinary actions, that may preclude imposition of identical federal discipline. The practitioner must raise a genuine issue of material fact on this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof and nature of the required showing
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent must "clearly and convincingly" demonstrate that there is a genuine issue of material fact as to one of the § 11.24(d)(1) factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office treats this standard narrowly; citations emphasize that the respondent's showing must be clear and convincing, and the question is whether a genuine issue of material fact exists — not a de novo reweighing of the state record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to state disciplinary proceedings; not a court of review
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director, like federal courts, is not sitting as a court of review to discover error in the state proceedings and generally gives state disciplinary orders due respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office will accept state findings unless one of the narrow exceptions is met. Evidentiary rulings, credibility determinations, and procedural judgments by the state panel are entitled to deference absent clear infirmities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions to assess penalty appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: The ABA Standards inform whether suspension or other sanctions are within the appropriate range for the adjudicated misconduct (e.g., Standards 6.3/6.32, 7.2, 9.1, 9.21-9.22).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office evaluates whether the state's chosen sanction is consistent with ABA Standards (e.g., suspension is generally appropriate when a lawyer knowingly communicates improperly and causes injury). The Office also considers whether aggravating and mitigating factors justify the sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors that can justify increased discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating circumstances include selfish or dishonest motive, refusal to acknowledge wrongful nature of conduct, vulnerability of the victim, lack of remorse, and similar factors (ABA Standard 9.22 examples cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of aggravating factors supports more severe discipline (e.g., the DHP cited selfish motive, refusal to acknowledge wrongful conduct, and victim vulnerability). The Office will consider these in determining whether the state's sanction is reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors and their limited role in reciprocal imposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating circumstances (and rehabilitative steps) may be considered in imposing discipline or for reinstatement but generally do not prevent imposition of reciprocal discipline absent a narrow showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although mitigation can affect sanction, for purposes of § 11.24 the question is whether the state's sanction is so ill-fitted as to be a grave injustice. Evidence of mitigation is often insufficient to rebut the presumption of reciprocity unless it bears directly on one of the § 11.24(d)(1) factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific misconduct rules forming basis for reciprocal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal discipline may be predicated upon violations of professional conduct rules (e.g., Missouri Rules 4-4.2: communicating with a person known to be represented by counsel about subject matter; and 4-8.4(d): engaging in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office examines the state's factual findings showing the rule violations (e.g., direct contact after being warned, letters causing harassment/threats). Such conduct, when proven, fits within ABA Standards supporting suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of administrative and public actions accompanying discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: If reciprocal discipline is imposed, the OED Director will publish a Notice in the Official Gazette, notify state disciplinary agencies and courts, and make the disciplinary decision publicly available (see 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.59, 11.24).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative measures may also include dissociation of the respondent's name from USPTO Customer Numbers and revocation/association changes to PKI certificates, and public notice to admissions jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties during suspension and restrictions on USPTO account access
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent must comply with duties enumerated in 37 C.F.R. § 11.58; USPTO will dissociate the respondent's name from any Customer Numbers and PKI certificates; respondent shall not apply for or obtain a USPTO Customer Number while suspended (unless reinstated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These operational requirements accompany suspension to prevent practice before the Office during the disciplinary period and to protect USPTO systems and clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for seeking reinstatement before the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent may seek reinstatement pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.60 after serving the specified period; as a condition of granting a petition for reinstatement, respondent shall demonstrate a passing grade on the Multistate Professional Responsibility Examination taken within the two years immediately preceding the request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order here required passing the MPRE within two years before seeking reinstatement and compliance with § 11.60; rehabilitative steps may be considered under § 11.60 but do not negate the reciprocal discipline analysis under § 11.24.
